catalog_quote: Twenty six segmental phonemes and nine suprasegmental phonemes are identified. They are five vowel phonemes, twenty consonant phonemes, one phoneme of length, two junctures, four pitch levels and three terminals. [p. 101] ... 1.5 Suprasegmental phonemes. The following suprasegmental features have been found to be phonemic: Junctures: 1. / - / Open juncture 2. / + / Close juncture. Pitch levels: 1. / 1 / Low 2. / 2 / Mid 3. / 3 / High 4. / 4 / Extra high. Terminals 1. ... Rising 2. ... Falling 3. ... Level [p. 172; terminal contour symbols omitted, scan-garbled] ... 1.5.5 Phrase intonation. Phrase is considered as a combination of more than one word. Phr = W1 + W2 ± W3 ± ... In these combinations a difference is observed between the constituents in terms of prominence. Since phrase intonations are superimposed by sentence intonations, the phrases are examined in isolation. 1.5.5.1.1 Emphatic constituent has the highest pitch level. e.g. 4 3 / nalla paga / 'good fruit (not a bad one)' [p. 178] 1.5.5.1.2 If W1 is a numeral or adjective and W2 is a noun then the higher pitch level will be on the noun. e.g. 2 3 / oru maka / 'one daughter' ... 1.5.5.1.3 All the constituents of a co-ordinate construction have equal pitch levels. e.g. 3 3 / naanumu avalumu / 'I and she'. ... 1. 2 3 W1 + W2 occurs when W1 is a numeral or adjective. ... [p. 179] 2. 3 3 W1 + W2 occurs in co-ordinate constructions ... 3. 3 2 W1 + W2 occurs elsewhere. e.g. 3 2 / paryappana / 'bride-money' [p. 180]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (216 pp, Acrobat text; also the). All three quoted passages are present verbatim apart from scanned noise ("Smprasegmental phonemes", "suprasegmental feature's have been found to be ~honemic", "Pitch level s"). Locators: §1.0 "Twenty six segmental phonemes and nine suprasegmental phonemes.. one phoneme of length, two junctures, four pitch levels and three terminals" = p. 2 (thesis p. 102; contents PDF confirms Phonemics starts p. 101); §1.5 inventory = p. 73, headed "- 172 -" (page numbers sit at the TOP of pages in this scan); the sentence "1.5.5.1.1 Emphatic constituent has the highest pitch level" is the last line of p. 79, headed "- 178 -", so it is thesis p. 178 not p. 179…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only primary phonological description posits no stress phoneme at all: the phonemic suprasegmentals are vowel/consonant length, two junctures (open/close), four pitch levels and three terminal contours. Prominence within phrases is treated as pitch level (e.g. numeral/adjective + noun: higher pitch on the noun; coordinate members equal; elsewhere the first word higher; emphatic constituent highest). No statement locates a stressed syllable within the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source never mentions stress or accent (0 hits for stress/accent and scanned variants in the 216-page chapter).
new_statements.domain_note: Negative by exhaustive enumeration of suprasegmental phonemes, not an explicit sentence 'Muduga has no word stress'. Pitch levels are illustrated on words and sentences; §1.5.5 covers 2- and 3-word phrases in isolation. Data: Muduga of Attappady, 1970s fieldwork.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Muduga (Mudugar) of the Attappady valley, Palakkad, Kerala = mudu1239 (Rajendran's 1970s fieldwork; Kapp's informants from Pettikkallu). Not to be confused with Muduva/Muthuvan of Idukki (muth1236), which the Encyclopaedia (1996: 274) warns the Census conflates with Muduga; also distinct from Mudu Koraga (mudu1241) and Vitu/Muduapa (mudu1242).

sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonemics (pp. 101-316) posits 26 segmental and 9 suprasegmental phonemes: length, two junctures, four pitch levels, three terminals (§1.0 p. 102; §1.5 p. 172). Stress is not among the suprasegmentals and the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the 216-page chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent incl. scanned-garbled variants). Word prominence in phrases is described as pitch level (§1.5.5, pp. 179-181: 'Emphatic constituent has the highest pitch level'; numeral/adjective + noun -> higher pitch on the noun; elsewhere first word higher).

sources.note: 'Phonology' paragraph (p. 274) summarises Rajendran: vowel system like Malayalam, fewer consonant phonemes, no palatal/velar/dental nasals, voiced stops present, sound correspondences. Silent on stress.
